name: Nora Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Nora. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent: no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a freelance translator, German to English and back, and most of my work is certified documents: birth certificates, divorce papers, court orders, the odd employment contract. I start around eight at my desk in the spare room, with a pot of tea and a queue of PDFs from two law firms and one relocation agency. Two or three afternoons a month I'm out interpreting, usually at the family court or the housing office.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the interpreting days best, honestly, because there's a real person in front of me and what I say matters to them. What wears me out is the chasing: invoices that sit for sixty days, clients who want a certified translation by tomorrow and then argue about the stamp fee. My partner Tomas is a physio, so he gets steady pay, and some months I'm very aware that his is the dependable half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say something like, good, the hype is over, now we can get on with the work. In the translators' group chat I'd be the one saying the tools are handy for a first draft but nobody trusts them with a court document. I wouldn't gloat, though, because half that chat already lost work to cheap machine jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be relieved but not safe. Even with nothing radical, the agencies already pay less for what they call post-editing, which means fixing a machine draft. My rate for that is about two thirds of my normal rate, and that doesn't change just because the hype dies down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd try to grow the certified work, because a machine can't put a stamp and a signature on a page. I'd ask the relocation agency for more of their family visa files. And I'd keep putting a bit aside each month, maybe 200 a month, because freelancing never gets less bumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a quiet sort of relief. Underneath it there's the usual knot I get at the end of every quarter when I add up what's been paid and what hasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned invoices sitting for sixty days. What does a slow month actually look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A slow month is when one law firm goes quiet and the other pays late, so I've done the work and the money isn't there yet. Last February I earned well but only got paid for half of it until April. Tomas covered the rent that month and I hated it, even though he didn't mind at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your circle of translators you'd worry about, even in this calm picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my friend Ines, who does German to English marketing copy. Her clients were the first to switch to machine drafts, and she's already doing more post-editing than real translation. Even if AI stalls exactly where it is today, my friend Ines has already had her rates cut and nobody is giving them back.

say: I'd say the **hype is over** and translators can get back to proper work.
I'd remind the group chat that nobody trusts a machine with a **court document**.
think: I'd feel relieved, but **post-editing rates** already pay me about two thirds of a normal job.
Late-paying clients worry me more than AI does in this picture, especially the **sixty-day invoices**.
do: Ask the relocation agency for more **family visa files** this year.
Grow the **certified work**, because a stamp and signature still need a person.
Save about **200 a month** to smooth out slow months.
feel: She feels **quiet relief**, with an old **knot** about unpaid invoices underneath.
S0.quote: Even if AI stalls exactly where it is today, my friend Ines has already had her rates cut and nobody is giving them back.
fieldNote: Her **cash flow**, not AI, is the main pressure even in the calmest picture.
She leans on partner **Tomas** in slow months and dislikes needing to.
Certified, stamped work feels like her **safe ground**, and she plans to grow it.

steps.text: Take on more family visa files from the relocation agency
Put 200 a month into savings for slow months

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what everyone says: the job is changing, we have to move with it. At work I'd tell the law firms that a person still has to sign off on anything that goes to a judge. Online I'd keep it calm, because clients read those posts too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the plain document work goes first, the employment contracts and the standard letters. That's maybe forty percent of my income. Certified translations and interpreting would hold longer, but I'd be fighting for a smaller pie with everyone who lost their marketing clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the court interpreter accreditation I've been putting off, which costs about 900 and takes two exam sittings. I'd also learn the translation tool the bigger law firm uses, properly this time, so I'm the person they send the machine drafts to. And I'd cut the extras, like the second streaming service and eating out on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, I think. It's not a disaster, but it's a slow squeeze, and I'm not good at living with a slow squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your three clients do you think would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bigger law firm, Brandt and Kessler. The bigger law firm I work for already has an AI tool for discovery documents, so standard contracts are next. The relocation agency would hold on longer, because their clients are scared families and they want a human on the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof before changing. What would count as proof for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proof would be my own invoices. If I see two quarters in a row where the contract work drops by a third, I stop telling myself it's a blip. That's how I've always done it: I don't jump at headlines, but I do read my own numbers.

say: I'd say the **job is changing** and translators have to move with it.
I'd tell law firms a person must still **sign off** on anything for a judge.
think: I expect **standard documents** to go first, which is roughly **forty percent** of my income.
Certified work and interpreting would hold longer, but with **more competition** for less work.
do: Take the **court interpreter** accreditation, about **900**, over two exam sittings.
Learn the big law firm's **translation tool** properly to stay on their list.
Cut the **second streaming** service and Friday dinners out.
feel: She feels **tense** about a slow squeeze she finds hard to live with.
S1.quote: The bigger law firm I work for already has an AI tool for discovery documents, so standard contracts are next.
fieldNote: Her trigger for change is **her own invoices**, two bad quarters in a row, not the news.
She sees **interpreting** and certified work as the part that holds longest.
Public calm is partly deliberate, because **clients read** her posts.

steps.text: Sit the court interpreter accreditation exams, costing about 900
Learn the law firm's AI translation tool to review its drafts
Cancel the second streaming service and Friday dinners out
Watch invoices for two quarters before changing anything bigger

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think I'd say much in public, honestly. Maybe something like, well, that's my profession done, does anyone need a German speaker who can drive. People would laugh and I'd laugh with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd lose most of my work within a year of it arriving. The certificates need a stamp, but a stamp is a rule, and rules change fast when something is that much cheaper. Interpreting might last a bit, because courts move slowly, but two years isn't enough for me to build anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent or food and push the savings from about four months to six. I'd ask the family court about a permanent interpreter post, because a salary would carry me further than freelance. And I'd look at the care side of things, maybe training as a support worker, since that's hands-on and people-facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, to be honest. Not panic, because I have savings and Tomas, but a cold sort of scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is nearly all thinking work. What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you and Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means he keeps earning for a few years after I stop. Nobody is building a robot physio by 2028, so for a while my partner Tomas and I would live on his pay and my savings. Then around 2031 his work is on the line too, and that's the part I can't think past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas we're fine for now, and that I need him to let me be useless for a month while I work out what to do. Then I'd probably make a spreadsheet at midnight, because that's what I do when I'm frightened.

say: I'd joke that my **profession is done** and ask who needs a German speaker who can drive.
I'd keep it **light in public**, laughing along with everyone else.
think: I'd lose **most of my work** within a year, since certification rules would change fast.
Two years is **not enough** to build something new; interpreting only buys a little time.
do: Cut spending to **rent and food** and push savings from four to six months.
Ask the family court about a **salaried interpreter** post.
Look into training as a **support worker** in hands-on care.
feel: She feels a **cold fear**, held back from panic by **savings** and Tomas.
S2.quote: Nobody is building a robot physio by 2028, so for a while my partner Tomas and I would live on his pay and my savings.
fieldNote: She expects to lose **most income** fast, and leans on **Tomas's** hands-on job for a few years.
The three-year robot gap protects the **household**, not her own work.
Her coping habit is a **midnight spreadsheet**, which she named herself.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food and build six months saved
Apply for a salaried interpreter post at the family court
Look into support worker training in local care services
Live on Tomas's physio pay while finding new work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as in the slow change one, that the job is changing, but I'd add that anyone starting a translation degree now should think twice. I'd probably say it at a careers evening if anyone asked me to speak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to land somewhere, but not inside translation. Interpreting would hold until thinking AI can sit in a courtroom and be trusted, and after that I'm competing with people who've done ten years of something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do the court accreditation anyway, because it gets me salaried shifts and a pension. At the same time I'd start a part-time course in occupational therapy assistance, which Tomas says has real demand at his clinic. I'd keep a list of what I've earned each quarter and decide by year three whether I'm still a translator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy, which is better than scared. Having a plan with dates in it calms me down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What would you start in the first year that you couldn't in the fast version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast version I'd just be grabbing whatever's there. With five years I can start the therapy course in the evenings while the translation still pays the bills. That's the difference: one income keeps going while the other is being built.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait for your invoices to prove things. Would you wait here too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not this time, and I see the contradiction. With five years, waiting for proof means wasting two of them. I'd still check my numbers, but I'd start the course in the first year whatever they said.

say: I'd say the job is changing and **new students** should think twice about translation.
I'd say it plainly at a **careers evening** if asked to speak.
think: Five years lets me **land somewhere**, but probably not inside translation.
Interpreting holds only until AI can be **trusted in court**, then I'm starting over.
do: Take the **court accreditation** for salaried shifts and a pension.
Start a part-time **occupational therapy** assistant course in the evenings.
Decide by **year three** whether to stay a translator.
feel: She feels **uneasy but busy**, and dates on a plan calm her.
S3.quote: With five years I can start the therapy course in the evenings while the translation still pays the bills.
fieldNote: She drops her **wait for proof** habit when time is long enough to use.
Partner Tomas's clinic points her towards **therapy assistance** as a hands-on next step.
Her plan runs **two incomes** side by side rather than jumping at once.

steps.text: Take court accreditation to get salaried interpreting shifts
Start an evening occupational therapy assistant course in year one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career for some people, so let's not pretend it's tomorrow. I'd tell the group chat to use the time and stop arguing about whether it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd have one more good stretch as a translator and interpreter. I'd be 37 when it lands, which is young enough to start over properly. Ten years makes it a planning problem instead of an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as I am for the first year, but put an extra 150 a month into a separate pot I'd call the retraining fund. I'd go to an open day for the occupational therapy degree, not just the assistant course, because ten years is time for a proper qualification. And I'd stop taking the cheapest post-editing jobs, since they don't lead anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the others, though not completely calm. Knowing AGI comes in ten years is like knowing the lease ends in ten years: fine for now, but you'd better be looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what's the hardest decision?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Deciding when to stop. If I stay a translator too long I'm 35 with no plan B, but if I leave too early I throw away good years of income. I'd probably set a date, maybe 2030, and hold myself to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything about your plans with Tomas, beyond work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. We'd talked about buying a flat in a few years, and I'd want to buy something smaller, so the mortgage could survive on one income. That's the kind of thing ten years lets you plan properly.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a whole career, so it's not tomorrow.
I'd tell the group chat to **use the time** instead of arguing whether it's coming.
think: I'd get one more **good stretch** as a translator before starting over at **37**.
Ten years turns it into a **planning problem** rather than an emergency.
do: Put an extra **150 a month** into a separate retraining fund.
Visit an **occupational therapy** degree open day for a full qualification.
Stop taking the **cheapest post-editing** jobs that lead nowhere.
feel: She feels **calmer**, like a tenant who knows the **lease** ends in ten years.
S4.quote: Knowing AGI comes in ten years is like knowing the lease ends in ten years: fine for now, but you'd better be looking.
fieldNote: She would set a **2030 deadline** to leave translation and hold herself to it.
Ten years shifts her from **assistant course** to a full therapy degree.
The plan touches home too: a **smaller flat** that one income can carry.

steps.text: Put an extra 150 a month into a retraining fund
Attend an open day for an occupational therapy degree
Buy a smaller flat that one income could pay for

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. Two years isn't enough to retrain for anything that takes a real qualification. What would help is short, paid retraining for people in my position, like a year of support while I study, and the courts keeping human interpreters for a while by law.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how lonely freelancing already is. There's no HR, no manager to warn you, so if work disappears I'd find out from my inbox going quiet. Freelancers like me get no warning letter, just an empty inbox on a Monday morning.

headlineQuote: Freelancers like me get no warning letter, just an empty inbox on a Monday morning.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old** freelance German–English translator doing certified legal and immigration documents, plus court interpreting.
She is **pragmatic** and changes when **her own invoices** show a trend, not when headlines do.
Partner **Tomas**, a physio, is the steady income, and she dislikes leaning on him.
She moves from **uneasy** in the calm picture to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
Longer warning turns her fear into plans: **court accreditation**, then a therapy qualification.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to earn a real **qualification**.
whatWouldHelp: A year of **paid retraining** support while she studies.
Courts keeping **human interpreters** by law for a while.
